natural: Eight metres away, Marie Curie is explaining to somebody in Frankfurt why a value date cannot be moved. She does not look up.
plain: Eight metres away, Marie Curie is explaining to somebody in Frankfurt why a value date cannot be changed. She does not look up.

natural: Negative is not hostile. It is the word the technique uses. She is the person whose job this rewrites and nobody has given her a reason to believe us yet.
plain: Negative does not mean hostile. It is simply the word the technique uses. Marie is the person whose job this project will change, and nobody has yet given her a reason to trust us.

natural: Leonardo is the one I would watch. High interest. Very important. Neutral.
plain: Leonardo is the one I would watch. High interest, very important, and neutral.

natural: People keep reading neutral as supportive. It is not. It is a man who has not decided yet.
plain: People keep treating neutral as supportive. It is not. It means a man who has not yet decided.

natural: Florence has arrived without anyone noticing and is reading the screen over your shoulder, standing, which is how she reads everything.
plain: Florence has arrived without anyone noticing. She is reading the screen over your shoulder, standing up, which is how she reads everything.

natural: Lorenzo is medium interest? He chairs the board that funded us.
plain: Lorenzo is listed as medium interest? He chairs the board that gave us the money.

natural: Medium interest, very important, neutral. He has eleven other projects and about forty minutes a year for this one. That combination tells me what to send him and how often, which is where the communications plan starts.
plain: Medium interest, very important, neutral. He has eleven other projects and about forty minutes a year for this one. That combination tells me what to send him and how often. That is where the communications plan begins.

natural: And my row says Positive.
plain: And my row says Positive.

natural: Positive, very important, high interest.
plain: Yes. Positive, very important, high interest.

natural: Optimistic of you. Ask me again in November.
plain: That is optimistic. Ask me again in November.

natural: It is not finished either. You have twenty-two rows and I can name six people in Finance and Control who are not on it, three of whom will be reconciling this thing at seven in the morning.
plain: It is also not finished. You have twenty-two rows. I can name six people in Finance and Control who are missing, and three of them will be checking this system's records at seven in the morning.

natural: Your afternoon is now spoken for, and Grace has already opened her calendar.
plain: Your afternoon is now fully booked, and Grace has already opened her calendar.

natural: Thursday, two hours, and I bring the divisional list. You will get names you would never have found and two you did not want.
plain: Thursday, for two hours, and I will bring the list of my division. You will get names you would never have found, and two that you did not want.

natural: Then you will list the people who come to meetings. That is a different list from the people who can stop you.
plain: Then you will list the people who attend meetings. That is a different list from the people who can stop you.

natural: You would be taking staff data collected for one purpose and using it for another. Ask me before you ask them, not after.
plain: You would take staff data that was collected for one purpose and use it for a different one. Ask me before you ask them, not afterwards.

natural: You will get forty replies saying High, and I will spend a fortnight ranking my own staff against each other.
plain: You will receive forty replies that all say High. Then I will spend two weeks ranking my own staff against each other.

natural: Fourth workshop in three weeks. Cold coffee, a whiteboard nobody has cleaned properly, and two hundred and fourteen numbered lines on the screen.
plain: This is the fourth workshop in three weeks. There is cold coffee, a whiteboard that nobody has cleaned properly, and 214 numbered lines on the screen.

natural: Requirement. Put a Refresh button at the top right of the disbursement queue.
plain: Here is a requirement. Put a Refresh button in the top right corner of the disbursement queue screen.

natural: That is a solution.
plain: That is a solution, not a requirement.

natural: It is a button.
plain: It is a button.

natural: It is a solution shaped like a button. Tell me the need.
plain: It is a solution in the shape of a button. Tell me the need behind it.

natural: I need to know that the queue in front of me is the queue that exists. At the moment I close the screen and open it again, twice, before I release anything.
plain: I need to know that the queue I am looking at is the real one. At the moment I close the screen and reopen it twice before I release any payment.

natural: That is a requirement. A loan administrator must be able to see the current state of the disbursement queue without leaving the screen.
plain: That is a requirement. A loan administrator must be able to see the current state of the disbursement queue without leaving the screen.

natural: Now the platform can satisfy it three ways and one of them costs nothing, because it is already in the product.
plain: Now the platform can meet that need in three ways. One of them costs nothing, because the product already does it.

natural: Write both. The need is the requirement. The button goes in the notes as the thing that prompted it.
plain: Write down both. The need is the requirement. The button goes in the notes as the thing that started the discussion.

natural: And the priorities, because everything Marie says is critical at the moment she says it.
plain: And the priorities, because everything Marie says sounds critical at the moment she says it.

natural: MoSCoW. Must, Should, Could, Won't. Won't is a decision, not a refusal — it means not this time, and it is written down so nobody re-argues it in 2027.
plain: We use MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have. Won't is a decision, not a refusal. It means not in this project, and it is written down so that nobody argues about it again in 2027.

natural: As of this morning, ninety-six Must, seventy-one Should, thirty-nine Could, eight Won't.
plain: As of this morning there are 96 Must, 71 Should, 39 Could and 8 Won't.

natural: Ninety-six Musts is not a prioritisation. It is a wish list with a ribbon on it.
plain: Ninety-six Must requirements is not a prioritisation. It is a wish list with a ribbon on it.

natural: Then come to the review and challenge them one at a time. A Must is a requirement without which we do not go live on the fifteenth of May 2028. Say that sentence over all ninety-six and about twenty will move on their own.
plain: Then come to the review and challenge them one by one. A Must is a requirement without which we cannot go live on 15 May 2028. Say that sentence over all 96 and about twenty will move down by themselves.

natural: I will come.
plain: I will come.

natural: The states matter as much as the priorities. Specified, Proposed, Approved, Incorporated, Implemented, Validated. Approved is the line that changes everything, because after it those requirements are the scope.
plain: The states matter as much as the priorities. They are Specified, Proposed, Approved, Incorporated, Implemented and Validated. Approved is the important line. After a requirement is approved, it is part of the agreed scope.

natural: And when I find something in 2027 that all of us forgot?
plain: And what happens when I find something in 2027 that we all forgot?

natural: Then you have not found a requirement. You have found a change.
plain: Then you have not found a requirement. You have found a change.

natural: Florence has been in the doorway for a minute and a half with her coat over one arm.
plain: Florence has been standing in the doorway for a minute and a half, with her coat over one arm.

natural: Somebody from a cabinet asked me in the lift this morning whether we could put backstop screens in.
plain: This morning, somebody from a Board member's private office asked me in the lift whether we could add backstop screens.

natural: In the lift.
plain: In the lift.

natural: In the lift. So read me section four point four, because I am going to have to say it back to him.
plain: Yes, in the lift. So read me section 4.4, because I will have to repeat it to him.

natural: Any deviation from the scope, schedule, cost or quality we baseline in June. Size and priority both scored one to five. Very low and low, Grace and I decide. Medium and above, the Steering Committee sits as the change control board.
plain: A change is any deviation from the scope, schedule, cost or quality that we approve in June. Size and priority are each scored from 1 to 5. For very low and low, Grace and I decide. For medium and above, the Steering Committee acts as the change control board.

natural: And four outcomes, not two. Approve, reject, postpone, merge. Postponed is an honest answer, which is why nothing has to be smuggled in.
plain: And there are four possible outcomes, not two. Approve, reject, postpone, or merge with another change. Postponed is an honest answer. That is why nothing has to be added secretly.

natural: He will hear that as no.
plain: He will hear that as a refusal.

natural: Then let him hear it from a form with a number on it rather than from you in a lift.
plain: Then let him hear it from a numbered form, instead of from you in a lift.

natural: Same room, new camera, no Legal. On the screen, a grid five squares by five, green in the bottom left and red in the top right.
plain: It is the same room, with a new camera and nobody from Legal. On the screen there is a grid of five squares by five. It is green in the bottom left corner and red in the top right.

natural: Likelihood times impact, each scored one to five. So the answer is somewhere between one and twenty-five. Two or below green, three to sixteen yellow, twenty and above red.
plain: You multiply likelihood by impact. Each is scored from 1 to 5. So the result is between 1 and 25. A score of 2 or less is green, 3 to 16 is yellow, and 20 or more is red.

natural: Invented by whom?
plain: Who invented those numbers?

natural: By this room, this afternoon, and then written into the plan so they are still the same numbers in 2028. Impact four means five to ten per cent of eight point four million, or several milestones moving.
plain: By this room, this afternoon. Then they are written into the plan, so they are still the same numbers in 2028. Impact 4 means 5 to 10 per cent of the 8.4 million euro budget, or several milestones being delayed.

natural: My risk appetite is zero. We are a crisis institution.
plain: My risk appetite is zero. We are a crisis institution.

natural: Then we stop this afternoon, because the only project with no risk is the one nobody starts.
plain: Then we stop this afternoon, because the only project with no risk is a project that nobody starts.

natural: Nobody says anything for a while. Outside, a delivery lorry reverses into the bay below with a great deal of beeping.
plain: For a while, nobody speaks. Outside, a delivery lorry reverses into the loading bay below, beeping loudly.

natural: Risk level six or below. Nothing above one chance in four. Nothing where the loss could run past two per cent of the budget.
plain: Then say: risk level 6 or below. Nothing with a likelihood above one in four. Nothing where the possible loss is more than 2 per cent of the budget.

natural: A hundred and sixty-eight thousand euro. That is now in the plan, and I will read it back to you in November.
plain: That is 168,000 euro. It is now written in the plan, and I will read it back to you in November.

natural: Categories, so the log sorts by something other than date.
plain: We also need categories, so the log can be sorted by something other than date.

natural: Six. Business. IT. People and organisation. External. Legal. Communication and information. The empty branches are the interesting ones, because they show where nobody has looked.
plain: There are six categories: business, IT, people and organisation, external, legal, and communication and information. The empty ones are the interesting ones, because they show where nobody has looked yet.

natural: Nobody has looked at legal.
plain: Nobody has looked at the legal category.

natural: Then take one from me. The platform contractor loses its lead architect halfway through. It has happened on every implementation I have run.
plain: Then take one from me. The platform contractor loses its lead architect halfway through the project. That has happened on every implementation I have managed.

natural: R-07. External, owner you. Likelihood three, impact four. Twelve. Yellow, above appetite, so we reduce it.
plain: That is risk R-07. Category external, and you are the owner. Likelihood 3, impact 4, so risk level 12. That is yellow and above the agreed appetite, so we must reduce it.

natural: We have not signed a contract. There is no architect to lose.
plain: We have not signed any contract yet. There is no architect to lose.

natural: No. Ignore that. That is precisely when it is cheap.
plain: No, ignore what I just said. This is exactly the moment when the response is cheap.

natural: A key-person clause in the tender documents, and Tesla shadowing the design authority from day one. Both of those are real work, so both of them will show up in the Work Plan with days against them.
plain: We put a key-person clause in the tender documents, and Nikola Tesla shadows the design authority from the first day. Both of those are real work, so both will appear in the Work Plan with a number of days against them.

natural: Then take mine. The parallel run is January to April 2028 and there is an EFSF rollover inside that window. My people cannot do both, and I have already been told which one comes second.
plain: Then take my risk. The parallel run is from January to April 2028, and there is an EFSF bond rollover in that period. My staff cannot do both. I have already been told which one will come second.

natural: R-11. Business, three and four, twelve again, and you own it. Escalation: six or below stays with me, eight to fifteen goes to Florence, sixteen and above to the Steering Committee. Red goes to Lorenzo's board as well.
plain: That is R-11. Category business, likelihood 3, impact 4, risk level 12 again, and you are the owner. Escalation works like this: 6 or below stays with me, 8 to 15 goes to Florence, 16 and above goes to the Steering Committee. Red risks also go to Lorenzo's board.

natural: And when one of them actually happens?
plain: And what happens when one of these risks actually occurs?

natural: Then it stops being a risk. A risk might happen. An issue has happened and needs a management action. It leaves one log and opens in another.
plain: Then it is no longer a risk. A risk is something that might happen. An issue is something that has happened and needs a management action. It leaves the Risk Log and is opened in the Issue Log.

natural: Do we log everything that goes wrong? Because things go wrong daily.
plain: Do we log everything that goes wrong? Things go wrong every day.

natural: No. Only what cannot be sorted out easily and needs a management action. Urgency, impact and size, one to five each. Small ones close with Grace. Medium and above go to the Steering Committee, and the decision lands in the Decision Log with a name against it.
plain: No. Only problems that cannot be solved easily and that need a management action. We score urgency, impact and size, each from 1 to 5. Small ones are closed by Grace and me. Medium and above go to the Steering Committee, and the decision goes into the Decision Log with a name next to it.

natural: So the day my architect walks out, R-07 becomes an issue and the whole room can see we saw it coming.
plain: So on the day my architect leaves, risk R-07 becomes an issue, and everyone can see that we expected it.

natural: And that we did something about it eighteen months earlier. That is what the yellow squares are for.
plain: And that we acted on it eighteen months earlier. That is the purpose of the yellow squares.

natural: Eighteen months. Put my appetite number in front of the Steering Committee in June. If I have to live with it I would rather five people watched me agree to it.
plain: Eighteen months. Put my risk appetite figure in front of the Steering Committee in June. If I must live with it, I would prefer five people to watch me agree to it.

natural: June, and the building's air conditioning has taken its usual position on the matter. W. Edwards Deming arrives with a printed checklist, a pencil and no laptop.
plain: It is June, and the building's air conditioning is not working well, as usual. W. Edwards Deming arrives with a printed checklist, a pencil and no laptop.

natural: Before we start. I do not work for you, and I do not report to you. I report to the Steering Committee.
plain: Before we begin: I do not work for you and I do not report to you. I report to the Project Steering Committee.

natural: I know. It is on my org chart in a different colour.
plain: I know. It is shown in a different colour on my organisation chart.

natural: Good. Objectives.
plain: Good. Tell me the quality objectives.

natural: Taken from the success criteria, not invented in this room. Disbursement five working days to one. Reconciliation three days to same day. Two open audit findings to zero.
plain: They come from the success criteria, not from this room. Payment time from five working days to one. Reconciliation from three days to the same day. Open audit findings from two to zero.

natural: Those are objectives. Now give me metrics with tolerances, or they are slogans on a wall.
plain: Those are objectives. Now give me measures with tolerances, or they are only slogans on a wall.

natural: Steering Committee monthly, tolerance one month. Every artefact reviewed once per phase, no tolerance.
plain: The Steering Committee meets monthly, with a tolerance of one month. Every artefact is reviewed once per phase, with no tolerance.

natural: A month of tolerance on a monthly meeting is generous.
plain: One month of tolerance on a monthly meeting is very generous.

natural: It is honest. Zero tolerance on something you will miss in August makes the whole document a lie by September.
plain: It is honest. If you set zero tolerance on something you will miss in August, the whole document is untrue by September.

natural: Can I have the communications plan before Johannes gets his folder tree out? Most of it is my meetings.
plain: Can we do the communications plan before Johannes shows his folder structure? Most of it is about my meetings.

natural: It is a table. Every meeting and every report, with audience, owner, frequency and medium. Status meeting Tuesdays. Core Team Thursdays. Steering Committee monthly, chaired by Florence, minuted by Grace.
plain: It is a table. It lists every meeting and every report, with its audience, its owner, how often it happens and the medium used. The status meeting is on Tuesdays. The core team meets on Thursdays. The Steering Committee meets monthly, chaired by Florence, with minutes written by Grace.

natural: Why not you?
plain: Why do you not write the minutes?

natural: Because I report into that meeting. The chair owns the record of the meeting she chairs, and it keeps the two of us apart on paper.
plain: Because I report to that meeting. The person who chairs a meeting owns its record. It keeps our two roles separate on paper.

natural: And a strategy per stakeholder rather than one broadcast. Lorenzo gets the progress report twice a year and nothing else. Marie gets a conversation before every acceptance, which is not a document at all.
plain: And each key stakeholder gets their own approach, instead of one message for everybody. Lorenzo receives the progress report twice a year and nothing else. Marie gets a conversation before every acceptance, which is not a document at all.

natural: That one I sign, then. Like the Handbook. Unlike the quality plan, which apparently belongs to my own committee rather than to me.
plain: So I sign that one, like the Handbook. But not the quality plan, which apparently belongs to my committee and not to me.

natural: Johannes Gutenberg has been waiting since ten past eleven with a folder tree open on his tablet. He turns it round without being asked.
plain: Johannes Gutenberg has been waiting since 11:10, with a folder structure open on his tablet. He turns it round without being asked.

natural: Twenty-six months from now, Internal Audit will ask which version of the interface specification the contractor was paid against. I would like to be able to answer.
plain: In twenty-six months, Internal Audit will ask which version of the interface specification the contractor was paid for. I would like to be able to answer that question.

natural: Configuration items: the Charter, the Handbook, the Work Plan, the interface specifications, the contract deliverables, the release packages.
plain: The configuration items are the Charter, the Handbook, the Work Plan, the interface specifications, the contract deliverables and the release packages.

natural: Number, name, CASTOR, date, version. Fifteen dot Quality underscore Management underscore Plan dot CASTOR dot twenty-six dash zero six dash twenty twenty-six dot v one point zero.
plain: The naming rule is: number, document name, CASTOR, date, version. For example: 15.Quality_Management_Plan.CASTOR.26-06-2026.v1.0.

natural: Folders 01 Initiating through 05 Closing. And a subject-line tag, because people obey a subject line and ignore a policy.
plain: The folders run from 01 Initiating to 05 Closing. There is also a tag for email subject lines, because people follow a subject line and ignore a written policy.

natural: Retention and sanitisation last. Agreed by Florence and Leonardo, implemented by me, reviewed by Brandeis.
plain: Retention and deletion come last. Florence and Leonardo agree them, I put them into practice, and Brandeis reviews them.

natural: And a registry. There is no PM² template for that one, so Gantt builds a spreadsheet and we walk it at every milestone.
plain: We also need a registry of these items. PM2 gives no template for it, so Gantt will build a spreadsheet, and we will go through it at every milestone.

natural: All of which is sensible. My question is narrower.
plain: All of that is sensible. My question is narrower.

natural: Which document does it go in? I have seen this filed in three different places in three different projects, and one of those projects could not prove anything at closure.
plain: Which document does it belong in? I have seen it filed in three different places in three different projects. One of those projects could prove nothing at closure.

natural: Gantt has the change plan open in one window and the quality plan in the other, waiting, with the cursor blinking in neither.
plain: Gantt has the change management plan open in one window and the quality management plan in the other. He is waiting, and the cursor is in neither of them.

natural: Correct, and now you know why I care about it. Configuration is how you prove at closure that what you accepted is what you paid for.
plain: That is correct, and now you know why it matters to me. Configuration management is how you prove at the end that what you accepted is what you paid for.

natural: Then my version numbers become change requests, and you will receive a Change Request Form every time I correct a typing error.
plain: Then my version numbers become change requests. You will get a Change Request Form every time I correct a typing mistake.

natural: I looked for it in March. There is no such template. There is not even a template for the registry.
plain: I looked for it in March. That template does not exist. There is not even a template for the registry.

natural: Then at the phase-exit review I have no evidence, and I will write that down in a sentence you will have to answer.
plain: Then at the phase-exit review I will have no evidence, and I will write that down in a sentence you will have to answer.

natural: Ten days to the baseline. The whiteboard has been wiped so many times it has gone grey, and somebody has written DO NOT ERASE across the top in a hand nobody recognises.
plain: There are ten days left before the plan is baselined. The whiteboard has been wiped so often that it has turned grey. Someone has written DO NOT ERASE across the top, in handwriting nobody recognises.

natural: Deliverables first. What the project produces. The work falls out of that, not the other way round.
plain: We start with the deliverables: what the project will produce. The work comes out of that, not the other way round.

natural: Configuration engine. Straight-through disbursement. A parallel run that proves both. A trained Lending Operations division. A decommissioned LOS.
plain: The configuration engine. Straight-through disbursement. A parallel run that proves both work. A trained Lending Operations division. And LOS switched off.

natural: How far down do we go?
plain: How far down should we break the work?

natural: Deliverables, work packages, activities, tasks. Far enough that somebody can be handed a task and know when it is finished. Not so far that I am tracking half-days in 2028.
plain: Deliverables, then work packages, then activities, then tasks. Deep enough that a person given a task knows when it is done. Not so deep that I am tracking half-days in 2028.

natural: Seven boxes at the second level, and they stay on that board all week. One point one, project management and PSO support. One point two, procurement and award. One point three, Release 1. One point four, Release 2. One point five, the parallel run. One point six, transition and go-live. One point seven, business implementation.
plain: There are seven boxes at the second level. They stay on that board all week. 1.1 is project management and support office work. 1.2 is procurement and contract award. 1.3 is Release 1. 1.4 is Release 2. 1.5 is the parallel run. 1.6 is transition and go-live. 1.7 is business implementation.

natural: Then under one point three. One point three point two, configure instrument templates. Under that, PCCL and ECCL. Then the loan facility. Then bank recapitalisation.
plain: Then under 1.3 there is 1.3.2, configure the instrument templates. Under that come the PCCL and ECCL templates, then the loan facility template, then the bank recapitalisation template.

natural: And the primary and secondary market facilities, which everyone forgets because we have not used them in years.
plain: And the primary and secondary market support facilities, which everyone forgets because we have not used them for years.

natural: Where is the backstop?
plain: Where is the backstop instrument?

natural: Nowhere. Out of scope at baseline, because the Treaty reform is not in force. It is a dependency in the Handbook and a requirement marked Won't. If ratification completes, that is a change with a form and a number.
plain: It is not there. It is out of scope at baseline, because the Treaty reform is not yet in force. It is listed as a dependency in the Handbook and as a requirement marked Won't. If ratification is completed, it becomes a change, with a form and a number.

natural: One point seven. Say out loud what it is.
plain: Now 1.7. Say clearly what it is.

natural: Retraining forty loan administrators and every business change around them. Two hundred and sixty days.
plain: It is retraining forty loan administrators, and all the business changes around that. It is 260 days of effort.

natural: Two hundred and sixty days of my people's lives, and it is my plan, not yours.
plain: That is 260 days of my staff's working lives. And it is my plan, not yours.

natural: It is your plan.
plain: It is your plan.

natural: That was apparently not the argument Grace had prepared. She stops, and starts again more slowly.
plain: That was clearly not the argument Grace had prepared. She stops, then starts again more slowly.

natural: Then say which document, because in April you told Marie the training was in the Transition Plan.
plain: Then tell me which document it is in, because in April you told Marie that the training was in the Transition Plan.

natural: I did, and I was wrong. Moving the old world to the new one — cutover, fallback, the day LOS goes read-only — that is the Transition Plan and I write it. The impact on your people, the retraining, the process redesign, that is the Business Implementation Plan and you write it.
plain: I did say that, and I was wrong. Moving from the old system to the new one — the cutover, the fallback plan, the day LOS becomes read-only — is the Transition Plan, and I write it. The effect on your staff, the retraining and the redesign of processes is the Business Implementation Plan, and you write it.

natural: And you assist.
plain: And you help me with it.

natural: I assist, and I put your activities in the Work Plan. Both plans land there in the end, which is why it is one number and one line of money either way.
plain: I help you, and I put your activities into the Project Work Plan. Both plans end up there. That is why it is one figure and one budget line, whichever plan describes the work.

natural: Different approvers, though.
plain: But they have different approvers.

natural: Different approvers. Florence signs hers. The Steering Committee signs mine.
plain: Yes, different approvers. Florence approves the Business Implementation Plan. The Steering Committee approves the Transition Plan.

natural: And the risk responses? The key-person clause. Tesla shadowing the architect.
plain: And what about the risk responses? The key-person clause, and Tesla shadowing the architect.

natural: In. Anything that costs real days goes in the breakdown, wherever it came from. Risk responses, corrective actions, quality reviews, the phase-exit checklists. If it costs days and it is not in here, it is not in the budget.
plain: They go in. Anything that costs real working days goes into the breakdown, whatever its source: risk responses, corrective actions, quality reviews, the phase-exit checklists. If it costs days and it is not in here, then it is not in the budget.

natural: You have nothing under the parallel run except running it.
plain: You have nothing under the parallel run except the act of running it.

natural: Then add it. Reconciliation evidence, the acceptance pack for Marie, and the fallback to LOS if the run fails. One point five point four. Write it down before somebody assumes it is free.
plain: Then add it. Reconciliation evidence, the acceptance pack for Marie, and the fallback to LOS if the run fails. That is 1.5.4. Write it down before somebody assumes it costs nothing.

natural: By four o'clock there are seven boxes, forty-one work packages and about a hundred and sixty tasks, and not one number against any of them.
plain: By 16:00 there are seven boxes, forty-one work packages and about 160 tasks. There is not a single number against any of them.

natural: Three days after National Day and the building is half empty. The Steering Committee is not. Florence in the chair, Grace taking the minutes, Albert Einstein present on request and saying nothing for the first eleven minutes.
plain: It is three days after National Day and the building is half empty. The Steering Committee is not. Florence chairs it, Grace takes the minutes, and Albert Einstein attends on request. He says nothing for the first eleven minutes.

natural: Item four. Ten days since the breakdown went on the wall. What changed?
plain: Item four. Ten days have passed since the breakdown went on the wall. What has changed?

natural: Every task has a resource or a resource profile against it. That is the step that turns effort into money. A task with nobody on it has an estimate and no price.
plain: Every task now has a person or a resource profile assigned to it. That is the step that turns effort into money. A task with nobody assigned has an effort estimate but no cost.

natural: We have not chosen a contractor. Award is the eighteenth of September.
plain: We have not chosen a contractor yet. The award is on 18 September.

natural: Which is why the contractor work is priced against a profile. Senior integration engineer, so many days, at the framework rate. When the team arrives the profile gets a name and either the number holds or I have a variance to explain in this room.
plain: That is why the contractor work is priced against a profile: senior integration engineer, a number of days, at the rate in the framework contract. When the team arrives, the profile gets a real name. Then either the figure holds, or I explain the difference in this room.

natural: And the estimates came from where?
plain: And where did the estimates come from?

natural: From the people who will do the work, with Tesla and Ada on both sides of it, and from the two comparable migrations Gantt found in the archive. Not from me alone with a spreadsheet.
plain: They came from the people who will do the work, with Tesla and Ada on both sides. They also came from two similar migrations that Gantt found in the archive. They did not come from me alone with a spreadsheet.

natural: Seven rows go up on the screen. Three columns of numbers and one total that everybody in the room already knows.
plain: Seven rows appear on the screen. There are three columns of numbers and one total that everyone in the room already knows.

natural: Project management, three hundred and forty days, five hundred and fifty thousand. Procurement, one hundred and sixty, two hundred and fifty thousand. Release 1, eight hundred and twenty, two point four million. Release 2, nine hundred and forty, two point eight million.
plain: Project management: 340 days, 550,000 euro. Procurement: 160 days, 250,000 euro. Release 1: 820 days, 2.4 million. Release 2: 940 days, 2.8 million.

natural: Parallel run, three hundred and sixty, one point zero five million. Transition and go-live, two hundred and twenty, seven hundred and fifty thousand. Business implementation, two hundred and sixty, six hundred thousand.
plain: Parallel run: 360 days, 1.05 million. Transition and go-live: 220 days, 750,000. Business implementation: 260 days, 600,000.

natural: Three thousand one hundred days. Eight point four million.
plain: That is 3,100 days and 8.4 million euro.

natural: Which is exactly the Charter figure. That is either very good work or a number you worked backwards to.
plain: That is exactly the figure in the Charter. Either that is very good work, or you calculated backwards from the answer.

natural: We met it by moving two hundred days out of Release 2 into the parallel run, and by cutting one point three point five entirely. Both are in the estimates section with a date on them. Ask me about any line.
plain: We reached it by moving 200 days from Release 2 into the parallel run, and by removing work package 1.3.5 completely. Both changes are in the estimates section, with a date. Ask me about any line.

natural: One point five. Three hundred and sixty days for the parallel run. In those four months my team is also reconciling an EFSF rollover.
plain: Take 1.5. It is 360 days for the parallel run. During those four months my team is also reconciling an EFSF bond rollover.

natural: That is R-11 and it is Grace's. The schedule shows the dependency rather than hiding it: the run cannot start before Release 2 is accepted, so if December slips, the run slides into the rollover and we are back in this room.
plain: That is risk R-11, and Grace owns it. The schedule shows the dependency instead of hiding it. The parallel run cannot start before Release 2 is accepted. So if December is late, the run moves into the rollover period, and we come back to this room.

natural: Show me the dependencies rather than the bars. Bars flatter everybody.
plain: Show me the dependencies, not the bar chart. A bar chart makes everyone look good.

natural: Procurement waits on project management. Release 1 on the award. Release 2 on Release 1. The parallel run on Release 2. Transition on the parallel run. Business implementation runs alongside from Release 2, and that is the one place we have deliberately taken a risk.
plain: Procurement waits for project management. Release 1 waits for the contract award. Release 2 waits for Release 1. The parallel run waits for Release 2. Transition waits for the parallel run. Business implementation runs at the same time from Release 2 onwards. That is the one place where we have deliberately accepted a risk.

natural: Then that is the line I would watch. Not the total.
plain: Then that is the line I would watch, not the total.

natural: And after today it is frozen.
plain: And after today it is frozen.

natural: Baselined. Not frozen. The baseline is what we measure against, the file stays current for twenty-six months, and every approved change re-baselines it.
plain: It is baselined, not frozen. The baseline is what we measure against. The file stays up to date for twenty-six months, and every approved change creates a new baseline.

natural: Florence turns the last page and does not sign it. She looks at you, then at the room, and puts the pen down on the table rather than in her hand.
plain: Florence turns to the last page and does not sign. She looks at you, then at the room, and puts the pen down on the table instead of holding it.

natural: This morning I signed the Handbook and the Stakeholder Matrix in my own office, on my own signature.
plain: This morning I signed the Handbook and the Stakeholder Matrix in my own office, with my own signature.

natural: So what is different about this one?
plain: So what is different about this document?

natural: Grace's pen has stopped. Whatever you say next goes into the minutes as the answer, and Deming will read it at the gate on the third of July.
plain: Grace has stopped writing. Whatever you say next will be recorded in the minutes as the answer. Deming will read it at the gate on 3 July.

natural: Then let the minutes show that the committee approves it. Grace, decision four. And the Quality Management Plan with it, since that one is also ours and not mine.
plain: Then record in the minutes that the committee approves it. Grace, that is decision four. Approve the Quality Management Plan at the same time, because that one also belongs to the committee, not to me.

natural: Then you are asking us to approve a calendar. We can all read a calendar without leaving our offices.
plain: Then you are asking us to approve a calendar. We can each read a calendar without coming to a meeting.

natural: And when Release 1 runs over, which line do we say it came out of?
plain: And when Release 1 costs more than planned, which line do we say the money came from?

natural: Convenient. Then the person who wants the benefits also signs off the effort my division has to find.
plain: That is convenient. Then the person who wants the benefits also approves the effort that my division must supply.

natural: Rain on the plateau since Monday. Behind Lorenzo de' Medici a tram slides down Avenue John F. Kennedy and disappears past the Philharmonie. He has given you forty minutes and looks like a man who intends to use twenty.
plain: It has rained on the Kirchberg plateau since Monday. Behind Lorenzo de' Medici, a tram passes on Avenue John F. Kennedy. He has given you forty minutes. He looks like he plans to use only twenty.

natural: Item three. Outsourcing Plan, draft zero point three.
plain: Item three on the agenda. The Outsourcing Plan, draft version 0.3.

natural: Before you read it. One sentence, in a document nobody can reopen. The platform is bought. Not built.
plain: Before you read it, I want one sentence in a document that nobody can argue with later. The platform is bought. It is not built here.

natural: Page two, first paragraph.
plain: That sentence is on page two, in the first paragraph.

natural: Four drafts have said that. On Friday somebody asked my architects to price a build option again.
plain: Four different drafts have said that. On Friday, somebody again asked my architects to give a price for building it ourselves.

natural: They are asked because they keep offering.
plain: People ask them because your architects keep offering to build it.

natural: They offer because nobody ever closed the question.
plain: They offer because nobody ever closed the question properly.

natural: It closed on the twenty-fourth of March. Option C. Lorenzo's board signed it.
plain: The question closed on 24 March. Option C was chosen. Lorenzo's board approved it.

natural: Bought from outside: platform licence, implementation, migration of fourteen years of LOS data, two releases. Kept inside: requirements, testing, the two interfaces, and anything that touches the audit trail.
plain: This is what we buy from outside: the platform licence, the implementation work, the migration of fourteen years of LOS data, and two releases. This stays inside the ESM: requirements, testing, the two interfaces, and anything that touches the audit trail.

natural: The audit trail stays. Good. That is the sentence.
plain: The audit trail stays inside the ESM. Good. That is the sentence I wanted.

natural: Then tell me why I am in the room. I do not sit on your Steering Committee.
plain: Then tell me why I am here. I am not a member of your Project Steering Committee.

natural: Courtesy, mostly. Your board authorises the award in September, and I would rather you saw the criteria than the invoice.
plain: Politeness, mainly. Your board approves the contract award in September. I prefer you to see the selection criteria now, rather than only the bill later.

natural: It is not a courtesy.
plain: It is not politeness.

natural: Henry Gantt turns his screen round. One row of a responsibility table, guide page forty-eight. Accountable, the Appropriate Governance Body. Consulted, the Steering Committee, the Project Owner, the Business Manager. Supporting, the Solution Provider. Responsible, the Project Manager.
plain: Henry Gantt turns his screen so everyone can see it. It shows one row of a responsibility table from page 48 of the guide. Accountable: the Appropriate Governance Body. Consulted: the Steering Committee, the Project Owner and the Business Manager. Supporting: the Solution Provider. Responsible: the Project Manager.

natural: That is wrong. I approve the Business Case, the Charter, the Handbook, the Work Plan, the acceptance plan, the transition plan, the business implementation plan —
plain: That is wrong. I approve the Business Case, the Project Charter, the Project Handbook, the Work Plan, the Deliverables Acceptance Plan, the Transition Plan and the Business Implementation Plan...

natural: Read the list again.
plain: Please read that list again.

natural: She reads it again. The Outsourcing Plan is not on it. It has never been on it.
plain: Florence reads the list again. The Outsourcing Plan is not on the list. It was never on the list.

natural: When an award goes wrong, nobody asks the project. They ask this floor, in a room with the auditors, how a contractor was chosen.
plain: When a contract award goes wrong, nobody asks the project team about it. They ask us on this floor, in a room with the auditors, how the supplier was chosen.

natural: And I am an S. Supporting. On the one plan that decides who builds my platform.
plain: And I am marked S, for Supporting. On the one plan that decides who builds my platform.

natural: You review it. You are then accountable for what the contractor does. Those are two different sentences.
plain: You review the plan. After that you are accountable for how the contractor performs. Those are two different things.

natural: And whatever you write in it, the procurement code wins.
plain: And whatever you write in this plan, the ESM procurement rules are stronger than it.

natural: What is the ceiling?
plain: What is the maximum amount?

natural: Eight point four million. All in.
plain: 8.4 million euro. That includes everything.

natural: And if the tender comes back at nine?
plain: And if the best offer in the tender is nine million euro?

natural: Then it comes back to you.
plain: Then it comes back to your board.

natural: Zero point three is finished Thursday. Where does it go?
plain: Version 0.3 will be finished on Thursday. Where do you take it?

natural: Bring the evaluation criteria with it. I am approving a method, not a supplier — and if you ever want me to approve a supplier, I will want to know what left the portfolio to pay for him.
plain: Bring the evaluation criteria with the plan. I approve a method, not a company. And if you ever want me to approve a company, I will ask what other project lost its money to pay for it.

natural: It approves almost everything, which is exactly why people put this one in front of it and nobody notices for two years.
plain: The Steering Committee approves nearly everything. That is exactly why people bring this plan to it as well, and nobody notices the mistake for two years.

natural: I have just read my own list out loud in front of three people. It is not on it. Do not put me somewhere the guide did not.
plain: I just read my list of approvals out loud in front of three people. This plan is not on the list. Do not give me an approval the guide did not give me.

natural: I would take it. That is the problem with giving it to me. My division wants a supplier who agrees with my architects, and somebody outside this project should be allowed to mind about that.
plain: I would sign it. That is exactly the problem. My division wants a supplier who agrees with my architects. Somebody outside the project should be allowed to worry about that.

natural: Thunder over the plateau at half past nine in the morning, which May does not usually do. The lights in Room Werner come on by themselves.
plain: There is thunder over the Kirchberg plateau at 09:30 in the morning. That is unusual for May. The lights in Room Werner switch themselves on.

natural: Eleven vendor presentations in Amsterdam last week. I know what good looks like now. Let me write the technical criteria.
plain: Last week I watched eleven suppliers present in Amsterdam. Now I know what a good product looks like. Let me write the technical criteria.

natural: What does good look like?
plain: What does a good product look like?

natural: A firm called Levallois Systems. Their engine configured a new instrument on stage in about forty minutes.
plain: A company called Levallois Systems. On stage, their software set up a new lending product in about forty minutes.

natural: On stage. With a prepared instrument, a demonstration dataset and no reconciliation.
plain: On stage. With a lending product prepared in advance, demonstration data, and no reconciliation at the end.

natural: Say that again. Slowly.
plain: Please say that sentence again, slowly.

natural: It can be done, so we are allowed to ask for it. We can ask for what we have watched a supplier do.
plain: It is possible, so we are allowed to require it. We can require what we have seen a supplier do.

natural: You have watched one supplier. Write the criteria around what that supplier does and the tender has a winner before it opens. Everybody else pays to lose.
plain: You have seen one supplier. If you write the criteria to describe what that supplier does, the tender already has a winner before it starts. The other companies spend money on an offer that cannot win.

natural: Nobody says the other thing for a while. Nikola Tesla's badge is a contractor's badge. Levallois pays him. He is sitting at the table where the evaluation criteria are being drafted.
plain: For a while nobody says the other problem out loud. Nikola Tesla has a contractor's badge. Levallois Systems pays his salary. He is sitting at the table where the evaluation criteria are being written.

natural: Nikola. You will not be on the evaluation panel.
plain: Nikola, you will not be a member of the evaluation panel.

natural: I have not asked to be.
plain: I did not ask to be on it.

natural: I know. I am putting it in the plan today, while it is still nothing, rather than in September when it would be a favour.
plain: I know. I am writing it into the plan today, while it costs nothing. In September it would look like a favour to someone.

natural: Then take my architecture note out of the file as well. It is the only honest document in it.
plain: Then also remove my architecture note from the tender file. It is the only honest document in that file.

natural: The note stays. It goes to every bidder on the same morning, with everything else you have seen since January. And the criteria come from the Charter, not from Amsterdam. Onboard a new instrument in six weeks — SC3, down from nine months. Zero manual re-keying — SC4, down from fourteen hundred fields a quarter. Neither sentence names anybody.
plain: The note stays in the file. Every company that bids receives it on the same morning, with everything else you have seen since January. And the criteria come from the Project Charter, not from the Amsterdam demonstrations. Set up a new lending product in six weeks: that is success criterion SC3, down from nine months. No payment fields typed by hand: that is SC4, down from about 1,400 fields every three months. Neither sentence names a company.

natural: Six weeks reads generously beside forty minutes.
plain: Six weeks sounds very generous next to forty minutes.

natural: Six weeks is what the Business Case promised the Board. We do not move a target because a sales engineer was quick.
plain: Six weeks is what the Business Case promised the Board. We do not change a target because one sales engineer worked fast.

natural: You asked me to check the framework.
plain: You asked me to check the framework contract.

natural: It covers everything. Four years of work has gone through it.
plain: It covers everything. We have run four years of work through it.

natural: It covers staff augmentation and infrastructure. Nikola's days come through it. A licensed lending platform with implementation and fourteen years of migration does not. There is no mini-competition to run.
plain: It covers extra staff and infrastructure. Nikola's working days are paid through it. It does not cover a licensed lending platform with implementation work and fourteen years of data migration. So we cannot hold a mini-competition under it.

natural: That is four months.
plain: That costs us four months.

natural: Four months already in the schedule. Open tender under the procurement code, section three point one, two paragraphs. Award the eighteenth of September, Release 1 the twenty-sixth of March 2027, Release 2 the seventeenth of December 2027 — dated in the plan, so the contractor has to hold people against them.
plain: Those four months are already in the schedule. It will be an open tender under the ESM procurement rules. That goes in section 3.1, in two paragraphs. The contract is awarded on 18 Sep 2026, Release 1 on 26 Mar 2027, Release 2 on 17 Dec 2027. The dates are in the plan, so the supplier must keep staff available for them.

natural: Who talks to them?
plain: Who is allowed to speak to the supplier?

natural: I do. Sole interface. Their project manager reports to me and escalates to the Steering Committee if he has to. I approve timesheets and purchase orders. Florence accepts deliverables. Your board authorises the award.
plain: I am. I am the only contact point. Their project manager reports to me, and goes to the Steering Committee only if he must. I approve timesheets and purchase orders. Florence Nightingale accepts the deliverables. Your board approves the contract award.

natural: And what do they hand over besides working software?
plain: And what do they give us besides working software?

natural: Configuration manuals, an operations runbook, the migration mapping, the interface specifications. Named as deliverables, so in 2028 they are an obligation and not a favour.
plain: Configuration manuals, an operations handbook, the data migration mapping, and the interface specifications. They are named as deliverables, so in 2028 they are a contractual duty and not a favour.

natural: Then weight the headings before an envelope opens. Not after.
plain: Then decide how much each criterion counts before any offer is opened. Not afterwards.

natural: Fixed in advance, in writing, and no one person able to move them. That is all the sentence in the guide is asking for, and it is the only protection the losing bidders get.
plain: The criteria are fixed in advance, written down, and no single person can change them. That is all the rule in the guide asks for. It is also the only protection the companies that lose will have.

natural: And in two years an auditor reads your criteria beside their brochure and finds the same eleven words. I would rather not spend that afternoon.
plain: And in two years an auditor will read your criteria next to their sales brochure and find the same eleven words. I would prefer not to spend that afternoon explaining it.

natural: They would be sharper. They would also be mine, and my employer is going to bid, and you would have to explain the difference to somebody who was not in this room.
plain: They would be better criteria. They would also be my criteria, and my employer will bid for this work. You would then have to explain the difference to somebody who was not in this room.

natural: Then the first written record of how we choose is written after we have met the people we are choosing between. Procurement will ask you for them anyway, in June, and you will write them in an afternoon.
plain: Then the first written record of how we choose is created after we have already met the companies. Procurement will ask you for the criteria in June anyway, and you will write them in one afternoon.

natural: Marie Curie has brought one sheet of paper to a meeting about a plan for 2028. It is an acceptance form from the LOS interface change in 2019. Under the word accepted, in her own handwriting: with reservations, see attached. There is no attachment.
plain: Marie Curie brings one sheet of paper to a meeting about a plan for 2028. It is an acceptance form from the LOS interface change in 2019. Under the word accepted she wrote, by hand: with reservations, see attached. Nothing is attached.

natural: That is what accepted meant last time. I would like it to mean something else.
plain: That is what the word accepted meant the last time. I would like it to mean something different now.

natural: Then we define it now. Deliverables Acceptance Plan, section four.
plain: Then we define it now, in section 4 of the Deliverables Acceptance Plan.

natural: In May 2026. For a platform we have not bought, from a contractor we have not chosen, against a release nobody has designed.
plain: In May 2026. For a platform we have not bought, from a supplier we have not chosen, for a release that nobody has designed yet.

natural: Write the criteria in 2027, when there is something in front of you.
plain: Write the criteria in 2027, when there is something real to look at.

natural: Then they get written to fit whatever arrived.
plain: Then the criteria will be written to match whatever the supplier delivered.

natural: Yes.
plain: Yes.

natural: AC-01 to AC-05. Five criteria, each with a metric, a tolerance and a named approver. AC-04 is reconciliation. Same day. Tolerance, zero unexplained breaks. Approver, the Project Owner.
plain: There are five acceptance criteria, AC-01 to AC-05. Each one has a measurement, a tolerance and a named approver. AC-04 is about reconciliation. It must happen the same day. The tolerance is zero unexplained differences. The approver is the Project Owner.

natural: Zero. Across four months of parallel running.
plain: Zero. Over four months of running both systems side by side.

natural: Zero unexplained. A break with an explanation is a break with an explanation.
plain: Zero differences that nobody can explain. A difference that we can explain is simply an explained difference.

plain: Those are two different sentences, and the second one must be in the document. I will write the measurement myself. Unexplained means: not closed in the reconciliation log by the next value date.

natural: Who takes the measurement, and with what?
plain: Who performs the measurement, and using what method?

plain: By sampling. We take a random selection of one quarter's instructions and compare them with what LOS produced.

natural: Then say who verifies and who accepts, because they are not the same person and last time everyone thought they were.
plain: Then write down who verifies and who accepts. They are not the same person. Last time everybody thought they were.

natural: You verify. Florence accepts. Her signature is on the note, not yours.
plain: You verify the result. Florence Nightingale accepts the deliverable. Her signature goes on the acceptance note, not yours.

plain: And who approves the plan itself?

natural: The Steering Committee. You chair it, so you will be in the room, but the approval is the committee's.
plain: The Project Steering Committee approves the plan. You chair that committee, so you will be there. But the approval belongs to the committee, not to you alone.

natural: What am I allowed to do when it is nearly right and there is a value date on Monday?
plain: What am I allowed to do when a deliverable is almost correct and a payment is due on Monday?

natural: Provisional acceptance. A short listed set of non-critical problems, each with a name and a date. Anything else is rejection, and rejection is an issue with a resolution plan behind it.
plain: You can give provisional acceptance. That means a short written list of small problems, each with a person and a date against it. Anything worse is a rejection. A rejection becomes an issue, and the issue needs a plan to fix it.

natural: Then the list has to be short enough to read out loud.
plain: Then the list must be short enough to read aloud.

natural: Twenty-five person-days. That is what the acceptance testing costs in my people's time, and it is not spare time, it is Lending Operations time during a parallel run.
plain: Twenty-five person-days. That is how much of my team's time the acceptance testing will cost. That time is not free. It is Lending Operations time, during a period when both systems are running.

natural: And write down which people. Two of us have reconciled an EFSF-era portfolio by hand. One of the two retires in March 2028.
plain: And write down which people are needed. Only two of us have reconciled an EFSF-era loan portfolio by hand. One of those two retires in March 2028.

natural: That is a risk with a date on it, not a staffing detail. Put it in the log this week.
plain: That is a risk with a date, not a small staffing question. Put it in the Risk Log this week.

natural: And acceptance runs per release. March 2027 and December 2027. Not one afternoon in 2028 when everything arrives at once.
plain: Acceptance also happens for each release. In March 2027 and in December 2027. It is not one afternoon in 2028 when everything arrives together.

natural: Florence has not agreed to anything. She is looking at the 2019 form, at four words in Marie's handwriting and the empty space underneath them.
plain: Florence has not agreed to anything yet. She is looking at the 2019 form, at the four words in Marie's handwriting, and at the empty space below them.

natural: You are asking me to agree what good looks like before I have seen anything at all.
plain: You are asking me to agree what a good result looks like before I have seen anything at all.

natural: Then I know in 2028 what I am allowed to refuse, and so does the contractor, and neither of us has to be brave about it.
plain: Then in 2028 I will know what I am allowed to refuse. The supplier will know it too. Neither of us has to be brave about it.

natural: Release 1 is a deliverable. If the criteria arrive after it, then the first thing we accept is accepted against nothing, and the contractor writes the standard by delivering it.
plain: Release 1 is itself a deliverable. If the criteria arrive after it, then the first thing we accept has no standard behind it. The supplier sets the standard simply by delivering something.

natural: Requirement one one four says reconciliation shall be automated. Tell me the number that makes it true, the range you will still accept, and whose signature closes it. The requirement does none of those three.
plain: Requirement 114 says that reconciliation shall be automated. Now tell me the number that proves it, the range you would still accept, and whose signature closes it. The requirement does none of those three things.

natural: Then in 2028 it is my opinion against a contractor's lawyer, on a Friday, with a value date on Monday. I would rather have a number.
plain: Then in 2028 it becomes my opinion against a supplier's lawyer, on a Friday, with a payment due on Monday. I would prefer to have a number.

natural: Johannes Gutenberg has brought a document box to an eight-thirty meeting. Inside are the acceptance forms from the 2019 interface change. Three of them are photocopies of photocopies.
plain: Johannes Gutenberg brings a document box to a meeting at 08:30. Inside are the acceptance forms from the 2019 interface change. Three of them are copies of copies.

natural: Nineteen of these should exist. Eleven are in the folder. Four are in somebody's mailbox. Four I cannot find at all.
plain: There should be nineteen of these forms. Eleven are in the project folder. Four are in somebody's email. Four I cannot find at all.

natural: This time they go into the repository the day they are signed, with a version number and a retention period.
plain: This time each form goes into the document store on the day it is signed, with a version number and a retention period.

natural: Before you tailor any checklist, take three sections out of the plan. The configuration procedure. The defect severity table. The test-evidence standard. All three are in the Quality Management Plan, approved on the ninth of June. Two versions of a rule is no rule.
plain: Before you adapt any checklist, remove three sections from the plan: the configuration procedure, the table of defect severities, and the standard for test evidence. All three are already in the Quality Management Plan, approved on 9 June. If a rule exists in two documents, it is not a rule.

natural: It points at them instead.
plain: The acceptance plan will refer to them instead.

natural: Point. Do not copy.
plain: Refer to them. Do not copy them.

natural: The checklist on the screen has nineteen lines. Four planning, six executing, two coordination, five on the quality of deliverables, two on communication. It asks whether things happened. It does not say what they should be.
plain: The checklist on the screen has nineteen questions. Four about planning, six about executing, two about coordination, five about the quality of the deliverables, two about communication. It asks whether things happened. It does not define what should happen.

natural: It has no responsibility row anywhere in the guide. Nobody approves it. It is your control tool and it lives with you.
plain: The guide gives this checklist no responsibility row at all. Nobody approves it. It is your control tool and it stays with you.

natural: Check eight. Provisional acceptance performed with a limited number of minor issues. Limited is not a number.
plain: Look at check number 8. It says: provisional acceptance performed with a limited number of minor issues. Limited is not a number.

natural: Two. Written into the plan, not into the checklist. Three is a rejection.
plain: Two. That number goes into the plan, not into the checklist. Three problems means the deliverable is rejected.

natural: Then I can use it.
plain: Then I can work with it.

natural: My people will not be tested twice. Either the acceptance testing and the quality control read the same evidence, or my team spends 2027 producing paperwork for two audiences.
plain: My team will not be tested twice. Either the acceptance testing and the quality control use the same evidence, or my team spends 2027 producing documents for two different audiences.

natural: Same evidence. Read by two people for two different purposes.
plain: The same evidence. Two different people read it, for two different purposes.

natural: And it costs effort, which is in the Work Plan or it is nowhere. Twenty-five person-days of user acceptance testing, sitting in the baseline since Friday.
plain: And it costs effort. That effort is in the Work Plan or it does not exist. Twenty-five person-days of user acceptance testing have been in the baselined plan since Friday.

natural: One more. Step seven.
plain: One more thing. Step seven.

natural: Outsourced work. The acceptance process goes into the contract.
plain: For work done by a supplier, the acceptance process must be written into the contract.

natural: Which moves a date. The tender file closes in July. The contract is signed on the eighteenth of September. A plan approved after that describes an acceptance process the contractor never agreed to.
plain: That changes a date. The tender file closes in July. The contract is signed on 18 September. A plan approved after that date would describe an acceptance process the supplier never agreed to.

natural: So it is finished before the tender, not before go-live. That is a different project.
plain: So the plan must be finished before the tender, not before go-live. That is a completely different timetable.

natural: Approved the twenty-sixth of June. In the tender file in July.
plain: It is approved on 26 June. It goes into the tender file in July.

natural: And the retention?
plain: And what about the retention?

natural: Ten per cent held back until final acceptance.
plain: Ten per cent of the price is held back until final acceptance.

natural: Held against a reconciliation number that depends on the quality of our own data. No serious bidder prices that without a caveat, and the caveat will cost you more than the retention is worth.
plain: Held back against a reconciliation figure that depends on how good our own data is. No serious bidder will price that without adding a condition, and that condition will cost more than the retention is worth.

natural: Then write down what we owe them. A retention against a number we only half control is a dispute with a date on it.
plain: Then write down what we must provide to them. A retention held against a figure we only partly control is an argument waiting to happen on a known date.

natural: Nobody settles it. It goes on the list for the July drafting session, which is how most of these things are actually decided.
plain: Nobody decides it in this meeting. It goes on the list for the drafting session in July. That is how most of these questions are really settled.

natural: The manuals are deliverables too, or nobody will ask for them in 2028.
plain: The manuals are deliverables as well. If they are not listed, nobody will ask for them in 2028.

natural: It goes to Marie's forty, to Leonardo's support team and to Levallois with the tender. Nobody should meet this plan for the first time on the day they are asked to sign under it.
plain: The plan goes to Marie's forty colleagues, to Leonardo's support team, and to Levallois Systems with the tender. Nobody should see this plan for the first time on the day they are asked to sign under it.

natural: Somebody has printed the 2028 disbursement calendar and taped it across the whole of one wall. Value dates in black. EFSF bond maturities in red. There are more red weeks than anyone expected.
plain: Somebody has printed the 2028 payment calendar and taped it across a whole wall. The payment dates are in black. The EFSF bond repayment dates are in red. There are more red weeks than people expected.

natural: Parallel run, eighth of January to the thirtieth of April 2028. Cutover the fifteenth of May. LOS read-only from the sixteenth.
plain: Both systems run side by side from 8 January to 30 April 2028. We switch over on 15 May. From 16 May, LOS can only be read, not changed.

natural: Four months of doing everything twice. On a live calendar. Say the rest of it out loud.
plain: That means four months of doing all the work twice, on a real payment calendar. Say the rest of it out loud.

natural: Every instruction goes through both systems and the results are compared before the four o'clock cut-off. If they disagree, LOS wins and we write down why.
plain: Every payment instruction goes through both systems. The two results are compared before the 16:00 deadline. If they disagree, we use the LOS result and we record the reason for the difference.

natural: Then name who does the comparing. It is not going to be the forty of us on top of the day job, and if it is, say that too.
plain: Then write down who does the comparing. It cannot be the forty of us on top of our normal work. And if it is, then say so clearly.

natural: Add the EFSF legacy portfolios as a third stream. Nine loans, all closed, and the oldest repayment schedules we hold. They will break the converter.
plain: Add the old EFSF loan portfolios as a third stream. There are nine loans, all closed. They hold the oldest repayment schedules we have. They will break the conversion program.

natural: A third stream is three months I do not have.
plain: A third stream would cost three months, and I do not have them.

natural: Then convert them first. Run them against LOS in October 2027, before Release 2, when breaking things is still free.
plain: Then convert them first. Compare them with LOS in October 2027, before Release 2, when a failure still costs nothing.

natural: You had the legacy portfolios in the last week of the parallel run, where a failure would have cost the cutover date. You cross it out.
plain: In your draft, the old portfolios were converted in the last week of the parallel run. A failure there would have cost the go-live date. You cross that out.

natural: That is better than what I had. It goes in the prerequisites.
plain: That is better than my version. It becomes one of the conditions that must be met first.

natural: Prerequisites, then. Release 2 accepted, seventeenth of December 2027. Legacy portfolios converted and reconciled. Four clean parallel-run weeks. Forty loan administrators trained by the thirtieth of April.
plain: So the conditions are: Release 2 accepted on 17 December 2027; the old portfolios converted and reconciled; four parallel-run weeks with no unexplained differences; and forty loan administrators trained by 30 April.

natural: Trained by whom?
plain: Trained by whom?

natural: Trained by the thirtieth of April.
plain: Trained by 30 April.

natural: That is not an answer to the question I asked.
plain: That is not an answer to the question I asked.

natural: Before you two start. Access rights.
plain: Before you two begin that argument: access rights.

natural: Production rights are re-issued from nothing at cutover. Every Levallois account closes the same weekend, including Nikola's, and support staff go in the same morning.
plain: At go-live, all production access rights are created again from zero. Every Levallois Systems account is closed that same weekend, including Nikola's. Support staff receive their access on the same morning.

natural: The borrower contact data. Names, telephone numbers and bank details, coming out of a fourteen-year-old system into a supplier's platform. Put the retention rule next to the migration, not in an annex. A backup you keep for seven years is seven years of personal data you are keeping.
plain: There is also the borrower contact data: names, telephone numbers and bank details, moving out of a fourteen-year-old system into a supplier's platform. Write the data retention rule next to the migration section, not in an appendix. A backup kept for seven years is seven years of stored personal data.

natural: And the weekend has to miss two things. An EFSF bond rollover and the Finance month-end close. Look at the wall — that leaves three weekends in May.
plain: The go-live weekend must avoid two events: an EFSF bond rollover and the month-end accounting close in Finance. Look at the calendar on the wall. Only three weekends in May are free.

natural: And on the sixteenth of May the platform stops being mine.
plain: And on 16 May the platform is no longer my responsibility.

natural: The fifteenth. Transfer of responsibility from the Solution Provider to the Project Owner, signed at cutover. After that it is Lending Operations and your division's level-two support, not the project.
plain: On 15 May. Responsibility passes from the Solution Provider to the Project Owner, and the transfer is signed at go-live. After that the platform belongs to Lending Operations, with second-level support from your division. It is no longer the project's.

natural: With ninety days of Levallois behind it, and then my division is alone with it. Which is exactly why I want the operations runbook named in the contract.
plain: There will be ninety days of supplier support after go-live. After that my division is alone with the platform. That is exactly why I want the operations handbook named in the contract.

natural: Rollback?
plain: And if it goes wrong?

natural: LOS kept warm to the thirtieth of June. Florence can order it, and only before the six o'clock value-date cut-off.
plain: LOS stays ready to use until 30 June. Florence can order a return to LOS, but only before the 06:00 payment deadline.

natural: Six in the morning.
plain: Six o'clock in the morning.

natural: Six in the morning. And none of this is scheduled in this document. Every activity in it goes into the Work Plan with effort and a name, or it does not happen.
plain: Six o'clock in the morning. And none of this work is scheduled inside this document. Every activity in it goes into the Project Work Plan, with effort and a person's name, or it will not happen.

natural: Then put a name against training, because right now it is your document, my people, and nobody's budget.
plain: Then put a name against the training. At the moment it is your document, my staff, and nobody's money.

natural: Four o'clock on a Thursday. Grace Hopper has a laptop open, a phone face down beside it, and two windows on the screen. Neither of them is the Business Implementation Plan. Month-end close is Tuesday and the Board note is Friday.
plain: It is 16:00 on a Thursday. Grace Hopper has her laptop open and her phone face down beside it. Two windows are open on the screen. Neither of them is the Business Implementation Plan. The month-end accounting close is on Tuesday and her note for the Board is due on Friday.

natural: Ask me on Monday.
plain: Ask me again on Monday.

natural: The Steering Committee sees all four plans on the twenty-sixth.
plain: The Steering Committee reviews all four plans on 26 June.

natural: Then take the training. Put it in your transition document. It is a go-live thing, it is already a condition of cutover, and you have written half of it anyway.
plain: Then take the training away from me. Put it in your Transition Plan. It is about go-live, it is already a condition for switching over, and you have already written half of it.

natural: It would take me two evenings.
plain: I could write it in two evenings.

natural: It would.
plain: Yes, you could.

natural: And the gate checklist would still have a line saying Business Implementation Plan, approved, and there still would not be one.
plain: And the gate checklist would still contain a line saying Business Implementation Plan, approved. And there still would not be one.

natural: Can I say the part nobody has said?
plain: May I say the thing nobody has said yet?

natural: Nobody has told the forty anything. What they have is a rumour from the sixth-floor kitchen that half the jobs go when the re-keying goes.
plain: Nobody has told the forty administrators anything. All they have is a rumour from the sixth-floor kitchen: that half the jobs will disappear when the manual typing disappears.

natural: I know.
plain: I know.

natural: That is exactly the thing I do not have four hours to write down properly, and it is exactly the thing that decides whether any of this works.
plain: That is precisely the thing I have no four hours to write down properly. It is also precisely the thing that will decide whether all of this works.

natural: Florence Nightingale is in the doorway. She has come for something else entirely and has heard the last two sentences.
plain: Florence Nightingale is standing in the doorway. She came for a different reason and has heard the last two sentences.

natural: Which plan is late?
plain: Which plan is late?

natural: Mine.
plain: Mine.

natural: Since when is it yours?
plain: Since when is it your plan?
